title: Exercise 1
statement: Suppose that 40% of customers buy fire insurance, 30% buy theft insurance, and 20% buy both fire and theft insurance. What percentage of customers buy either fire insurance or theft insurance, but not both?
solution_steps: Let \(F\) denote the event that a customer buys fire insurance and \(T\) the event that a customer buys theft insurance.
We are given \(P(F)=0.4\), \(P(T)=0.3\), and \(P(F\cap T)=0.2\).
The probability of buying fire insurance only is \(P(F\cap T^c)=P(F)-P(F\cap T)=0.4-0.2=0.2\).
The probability of buying theft insurance only is \(P(F^c\cap T)=P(T)-P(F\cap T)=0.3-0.2=0.1\).
These two events are mutually exclusive, so their probabilities add: \(0.2+0.1=0.3\).
Therefore, \(30\%\) of customers buy exactly one of the two types of insurance.
generalization: The event that exactly one of two events occurs is their symmetric difference, \(A\triangle B\). Its probability is \(P(A\triangle B)=P(A)+P(B)-2P(A\cap B)\). Subtracting the intersection twice removes both copies included in \(P(A)+P(B)\).

title: Exercise 2
statement: An integer is randomly chosen from \(\{1,2,3,\ldots,25\}\), with each integer equally likely. What is the probability that it is even or divisible by 5, but not both?
solution_steps: Let \(E\) be the event that the chosen integer is even and \(D\) the event that it is divisible by 5.
There are 12 even integers: \(2,4,6,\ldots,24\). Thus, \(P(E)=12/25\).
There are 5 integers divisible by 5: \(5,10,15,20,25\). Thus, \(P(D)=5/25\).
An integer satisfying both conditions must be divisible by 10. The only such integers are 10 and 20, so \(P(E\cap D)=2/25\).
The probability of satisfying exactly one condition is \(P(E\triangle D)=P(E)+P(D)-2P(E\cap D)\).
Therefore, \(P(E\triangle D)=\dfrac{12+5-2(2)}{25}=\dfrac{13}{25}\).
generalization: For a uniformly selected integer from \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the probability of being divisible by \(a\) or \(b\), but not both, is \(\dfrac{\lfloor n/a\rfloor+\lfloor n/b\rfloor-2\lfloor n/\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\rfloor}{n}\). The common multiples are counted using the least common multiple.

title: Exercise 3
statement: If \(P(A)=0.3\) and \(P(B)=0.4\), what is the maximum possible value of \(P(A\cup B)\)?
solution_steps: Use the addition rule: \(P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)\).
Substituting the given probabilities gives \(P(A\cup B)=0.7-P(A\cap B)\).
To maximize the union probability, minimize the intersection probability.
Since \(P(A\cap B)\geq 0\), we have \(P(A\cup B)\leq 0.7\).
This bound is attainable when \(A\) and \(B\) are mutually exclusive: assign probability 0.3 to \(A\), 0.4 to \(B\), and 0.3 to neither event.
Therefore, the maximum possible value is \(0.7\).
generalization: For two events with given marginal probabilities, \(\max\{P(A),P(B)\}\leq P(A\cup B)\leq\min\{1,P(A)+P(B)\}\). The maximum union probability is obtained by minimizing the overlap. If \(P(A)+P(B)\leq 1\), mutually exclusive events attain the maximum.

title: Exercise 4
statement:
[SOA/CAS 1999 Practice Exam #1] A marketing survey indicates that 60% of the population owns an automobile, 30% owns a house, and 20% owns both an automobile and a house.

Calculate the probability that a person chosen at random owns an automobile or a house, but not both.
solution_steps: Let \(A\) denote automobile ownership and \(H\) house ownership.
We are given \(P(A)=0.6\), \(P(H)=0.3\), and \(P(A\cap H)=0.2\).
The probability of owning an automobile but no house is \(P(A\cap H^c)=0.6-0.2=0.4\).
The probability of owning a house but no automobile is \(P(A^c\cap H)=0.3-0.2=0.1\).
Add these mutually exclusive possibilities: \(P(A\triangle H)=0.4+0.1=0.5\).
Equivalently, \(P(A\triangle H)=0.6+0.3-2(0.2)=0.5\).
generalization: Distinguish 'at least one' from 'exactly one.' For two events, \(P(\text{at least one})=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)\), whereas \(P(\text{exactly one})=P(A)+P(B)-2P(A\cap B)\).

title: Exercise 5
statement: If \(P(A)=0.7\) and \(P(B)=0.6\), what is the minimum possible value of \(P(A\cap B)\)?
solution_steps: Rearrange the addition rule: \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cup B)\).
Substituting gives \(P(A\cap B)=1.3-P(A\cup B)\).
Every probability is at most 1, so \(P(A\cup B)\leq 1\). Consequently, \(P(A\cap B)\geq 1.3-1=0.3\).
To verify that this bound is attainable, assign probabilities \(P(A\cap B)=0.3\), \(P(A\cap B^c)=0.4\), \(P(A^c\cap B)=0.3\), and \(P(A^c\cap B^c)=0\).
These four probabilities are nonnegative and sum to 1. They also give \(P(A)=0.3+0.4=0.7\) and \(P(B)=0.3+0.3=0.6\).
Therefore, the minimum possible intersection probability is \(0.3\).
generalization: For any two events, \(\max\{0,P(A)+P(B)-1\}\leq P(A\cap B)\leq\min\{P(A),P(B)\}\). When the marginal probabilities sum to more than 1, an overlap of at least \(P(A)+P(B)-1\) is unavoidable. Independence must not be assumed unless stated.

title: Exercise 6
statement: If \(P(A)=0.7\) and \(P(B)=0.6\), what is the maximum possible value of \(P(A\cap B)\)?
solution_steps: The intersection is contained in each event: \(A\cap B\subseteq A\) and \(A\cap B\subseteq B\).
Therefore, \(P(A\cap B)\leq P(A)=0.7\) and \(P(A\cap B)\leq P(B)=0.6\).
The tighter bound is \(P(A\cap B)\leq\min\{0.7,0.6\}=0.6\).
This upper bound is attainable when \(B\subseteq A\). In this case, \(A\cap B=B\), so the intersection probability is 0.6.
For example, assign probability 0.6 to both events, 0.1 to \(A\) only, 0 to \(B\) only, and 0.3 to neither event.
Therefore, the maximum possible intersection probability is \(0.6\).
generalization: The largest possible intersection probability is \(\min\{P(A),P(B)\}\). It is attained when the event with the smaller probability is contained in the other event. The product \(P(A)P(B)\) applies under independence, which is a separate assumption.

title: Exercise 7
statement: If \(P(A)=0.3\) and \(P(B)=0.4\), what is the minimum possible value of \(P(A\cup B)\)?
solution_steps: The union contains both events, so \(P(A\cup B)\geq P(A)\) and \(P(A\cup B)\geq P(B)\).
Therefore, \(P(A\cup B)\geq\max\{0.3,0.4\}=0.4\).
Equivalently, the addition rule gives \(P(A\cup B)=0.7-P(A\cap B)\). Minimizing the union requires maximizing the intersection.
The maximum possible intersection probability is \(\min\{0.3,0.4\}=0.3\), giving \(P(A\cup B)=0.7-0.3=0.4\).
This bound is attainable when \(A\subseteq B\). Then \(A\cup B=B\), whose probability is 0.4.
Therefore, the minimum possible union probability is \(0.4\).
generalization: The smallest possible union probability is \(\max\{P(A),P(B)\}\). It is attained when the smaller-probability event is contained in the larger one. In general, \(\max\{P(A),P(B)\}\leq P(A\cup B)\leq\min\{1,P(A)+P(B)\}\).

title: Exercise 8
statement:
An analysis of an insurance company's policyholders finds the following:

i. Twice as many policyholders buy auto insurance as buy home insurance.
ii. 70% of policyholders buy either auto insurance or home insurance.
iii. 20% of policyholders buy both auto insurance and home insurance.

What fraction of policyholders buy home insurance but not auto insurance?
solution_steps: Let \(A\) denote buying auto insurance and \(H\) buying home insurance. We are given \(P(A)=2P(H)\), \(P(A\cup H)=0.7\), and \(P(A\cap H)=0.2\).
Here, 'either auto insurance or home insurance' describes the inclusive union, which includes policyholders who buy both.
Apply the addition rule: \(P(A\cup H)=P(A)+P(H)-P(A\cap H)\).
Substituting gives \(0.7=2P(H)+P(H)-0.2\), so \(3P(H)=0.9\) and \(P(H)=0.3\).
Home insurance but not auto insurance is the event \(H\cap A^c\). Its probability is \(P(H\cap A^c)=P(H)-P(A\cap H)=0.3-0.2=0.1\).
Therefore, the required fraction is \(10.0\%\).
generalization: If \(P(A)=kP(B)\), \(P(A\cup B)=u\), and \(P(A\cap B)=q\), then \(P(B)=(u+q)/(k+1)\). The probability of B only is \(P(B\cap A^c)=P(B)-q\).

title: Exercise 9
statement: You are given that \(P(A\cap B^c)=0.3\) and \(P((A\cup B)^c)=0.4\). What is \(P(B)\)?
solution_steps: By De Morgan's law, \((A\cup B)^c=A^c\cap B^c\). Hence, \(P(A^c\cap B^c)=0.4\).
Partition \(B^c\) according to whether A occurs: \(B^c=(A\cap B^c)\cup(A^c\cap B^c)\).
These two regions are disjoint, so \(P(B^c)=P(A\cap B^c)+P(A^c\cap B^c)=0.3+0.4=0.7\).
Using the complement rule gives \(P(B)=1-P(B^c)=1-0.7=0.3\).
generalization: Any event B can be partitioned using another event A: \(P(B)=P(A\cap B)+P(A^c\cap B)\). Similarly, \(P(B)=1-P(A\cap B^c)-P(A^c\cap B^c)\).

title: Exercise 10
statement:
[SOA 5; F00.03] An auto insurance company has 10,000 policyholders. Each policyholder is classified as:

i. young or old;
ii. male or female; and
iii. married or single.

Of these policyholders, 3,000 are young, 4,600 are male, and 7,000 are married. The policyholders can also be classified as 1,320 young males, 3,010 married males, and 1,400 young married persons. Finally, 600 of the policyholders are young married males.

How many of the company's policyholders are young, female, and single?
solution_steps: Let Y denote young policyholders, M male policyholders, and R married policyholders. We seek the number in \(Y\cap M^c\cap R^c\).
There are 3,000 young policyholders, of whom 1,320 are male. Therefore, there are \(3000-1320=1680\) young female policyholders.
There are 1,400 young married policyholders, of whom 600 are male. Therefore, there are \(1400-600=800\) young married female policyholders.
Subtract young married females from all young females: \(1680-800=880\).
Equivalently, inclusion-exclusion within Y gives \(|Y\cap M^c\cap R^c|=|Y|-|Y\cap M|-|Y\cap R|+|Y\cap M\cap R|\).
Substituting gives \(3000-1320-1400+600=880\). The overall counts of male and married policyholders are not needed.
generalization: To count members of A who belong to neither B nor C, use \(|A\cap B^c\cap C^c|=|A|-|A\cap B|-|A\cap C|+|A\cap B\cap C|\). Add back the triple intersection because it was subtracted twice.

title: Exercise 11
statement:
[SOA 100] A survey of 100 TV watchers revealed that over the last year:

i. 34 watched CBS.
ii. 15 watched NBC.
iii. 10 watched ABC.
iv. 7 watched CBS and NBC.
v. 6 watched CBS and ABC.
vi. 5 watched NBC and ABC.
vii. 4 watched CBS, NBC, and ABC.
viii. 18 watched HGTV and of these, none watched CBS, NBC, or ABC.

Calculate how many of the 100 TV watchers did not watch any of the four channels (CBS, NBC, ABC, or HGTV).
solution_steps: Let C, N, A, and H denote the sets of viewers who watched CBS, NBC, ABC, and HGTV, respectively.
Use inclusion-exclusion for the first three channels: \(|C\cup N\cup A|=|C|+|N|+|A|-|C\cap N|-|C\cap A|-|N\cap A|+|C\cap N\cap A|\).
Substituting gives \(|C\cup N\cup A|=34+15+10-7-6-5+4=45\).
The pairwise intersection counts include the viewers who watched all three channels. The triple intersection must therefore be added back once.
None of the 18 HGTV viewers watched any of the other three channels, so \(|C\cup N\cup A\cup H|=45+18=63\).
The number who watched none of the four channels is \(100-63=37\).
generalization: For three events, \(P(A\cup B\cup C)=P(A)+P(B)+P(C)-P(A\cap B)-P(A\cap C)-P(B\cap C)+P(A\cap B\cap C)\). The same identity holds for finite set counts. To find how many belong to none of the sets, subtract the union count from the total.

title: Exercise 12
statement:
Suppose that A, B, and C are events such that:

i. \(P(A)=0.6\) and \(P(B)=P(C)=0.5\).
ii. \(P(A\cap B)=P(A\cap C)=0.3\), but \(P(B\cap C)=0.2\).
iii. \(P(A\cap B\cap C)=0.1\).

Find \(P(A^c\cap B^c\cap C)\).
solution_steps: The event \(A^c\cap B^c\cap C\) means that C occurs while neither A nor B occurs. This is the C-only region.
Start with all of C, subtract its overlap with A and its overlap with B, then add back the triple intersection.
Thus, \(P(A^c\cap B^c\cap C)=P(C)-P(A\cap C)-P(B\cap C)+P(A\cap B\cap C)\).
Substituting gives \(0.5-0.3-0.2+0.1=0.1\).
The triple intersection is added back because it belongs to both subtracted intersections and would otherwise be removed twice.
generalization: For any three events, \(P(C\cap A^c\cap B^c)=P(C)-P(C\cap A)-P(C\cap B)+P(A\cap B\cap C)\). This is inclusion-exclusion applied within C.

title: Exercise 13
solution_steps: By De Morgan's law, \(A^c\cup B^c=(A\cap B)^c\).
This event includes every outcome except those in which both A and B occur.
Apply the complement rule: \(P(A^c\cup B^c)=1-P(A\cap B)\).
Therefore, \(P(A^c\cup B^c)=1-0.2=0.8\). The individual probabilities of A and B are not needed.
generalization: De Morgan's laws give \(A^c\cup B^c=(A\cap B)^c\) and \(A^c\cap B^c=(A\cup B)^c\). Consequently, 'not both' has probability \(1-P(A\cap B)\), while 'neither' has probability \(1-P(A\cup B)\).

title: Exercise 14
statement: Let X be the sum of the roll of two fair six-sided dice. Find \(P(X=8\mid X=7\text{ or }X=8)\).
solution_steps: The two dice are rolled independently, giving 36 equally likely ordered outcomes.
The events \(X=7\) and \(X=8\) are mutually exclusive, so \(P(X=7\text{ or }X=8)=11/36\).
Since \(\{X=8\}\subseteq\{X=7\text{ or }X=8\}\), conditional probability gives \(P(X=8\mid X=7\text{ or }X=8)=\dfrac{5/36}{11/36}=\dfrac{5}{11}\).
The two possible sums are not equally likely. Conditioning restricts the sample space to 11 equally likely ordered outcomes, five of which have sum 8.
generalization: If \(A\subseteq B\) and \(P(B)>0\), then \(P(A\mid B)=P(A)/P(B)\). In a finite equally likely sample space, conditional probability can be computed by counting favorable outcomes within the conditioning event.

title: Exercise 15
statement:
[SOA 9; S03.05] An insurance company examines its pool of auto insurance customers and gathers the following information:

i. All customers insure at least one car.
ii. 70% of customers insure more than one car.
iii. 20% of the customers insure a sports car.
iv. Of those customers who insure more than one car, 15% insure a sports car.

Calculate the probability that a randomly selected customer insures exactly one car and that car is not a sports car.
solution_steps: Let M denote insuring more than one car and S denote insuring a sports car. We are given \(P(M)=0.7\), \(P(S)=0.2\), and \(P(S\mid M)=0.15\).
Because every customer insures at least one car, \(M^c\) means insuring exactly one car. Thus, \(P(M^c)=1-0.7=0.3\).
Convert the conditional probability into a joint probability: \(P(M\cap S)=P(M)P(S\mid M)=0.7(0.15)=0.105\).
Partition sports-car customers by number of cars: \(P(M^c\cap S)=P(S)-P(M\cap S)=0.2-0.105=0.095\).
Among the customers who insure exactly one car, remove those whose car is a sports car: \(P(M^c\cap S^c)=0.3-0.095=0.205\).
The exact probability is \(0.205\), or \(20.5\%\). Rounded to two decimal places, it is \(0.21\), corresponding to choice B.
generalization: Given \(P(A)\), \(P(B)\), and \(P(B\mid A)\), first compute \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B\mid A)\). Then \(P(A^c\cap B^c)=1-P(A)-P(B)+P(A)P(B\mid A)\). A conditional percentage must be multiplied by the probability of its conditioning group.

title: Exercise 16
statement:
[SOA 10; F00.30] An actuary studying the insurance preferences of automobile owners makes the following conclusions:

i. An automobile owner is twice as likely to purchase collision coverage as disability coverage.
ii. The event that an automobile owner purchases collision coverage is independent of the event that he or she purchases disability coverage.
iii. The probability that an automobile owner purchases both collision and disability coverages is 0.15.

What is the probability that an automobile owner purchases neither collision nor disability coverage?
solution_steps: Let C denote purchasing collision coverage and D purchasing disability coverage. Write \(P(D)=d\), so \(P(C)=2d\).
By independence, \(P(C\cap D)=P(C)P(D)=2d^2\). The given intersection probability implies \(2d^2=0.15\).
Since d is a probability, take the nonnegative root: \(d=\sqrt{0.15/2}=\sqrt{0.075}\approx0.273861\).
Therefore, \(P(C)=2\sqrt{0.075}\approx0.547723\).
The probability of neither coverage is \(P(C^c\cap D^c)=1-P(C\cup D)=1-P(C)-P(D)+P(C\cap D)\).
Substituting without intermediate rounding gives \(P(C^c\cap D^c)=1.15-3\sqrt{0.075}\approx0.328416\).
Rounded to two decimal places, the required probability is \(0.33\). As a check, independence also gives \(P(C^c\cap D^c)=(1-P(C))(1-P(D))\).
generalization: If A and B are independent, \(P(A)=kP(B)\) with \(k>0\), and \(P(A\cap B)=q\), then \(P(B)=\sqrt{q/k}\) and \(P(A)=\sqrt{kq}\), provided these values are valid probabilities. Their complements are also independent, so \(P(A^c\cap B^c)=(1-P(A))(1-P(B))\).

title: Exercise 25
statement:
[SOA 25; F00.22] The probability that a randomly chosen male has a circulation problem is 0.25. Males who have a circulation problem are twice as likely to be smokers as those who do not have a circulation problem.

What is the conditional probability that a male has a circulation problem given that he is a smoker?
solution_steps: Let \(C\) denote having a circulation problem and \(S\) denote being a smoker. We know \(P(C)=0.25\) and \(P(C^c)=0.75\).
Set \(q=P(S\mid C^c)\). The statement gives \(P(S\mid C)=2q\).
By the law of total probability, \(P(S)=P(S\mid C)P(C)+P(S\mid C^c)P(C^c)=2q(0.25)+q(0.75)=1.25q\).
The joint probability is \(P(C\cap S)=P(C)P(S\mid C)=0.25(2q)=0.50q\).
Therefore, assuming \(P(S)>0\), \(P(C\mid S)=\frac{0.50q}{1.25q}=\frac{2}{5}=0.40\).
generalization: If \(P(A)=p\) and \(P(B\mid A)=rP(B\mid A^c)\), then Bayes' theorem gives \(P(A\mid B)=\frac{rp}{rp+1-p}\), provided \(P(B)>0\). The unknown common factor cancels.

title: Exercise 26
statement:
[SOA 19; S01.06] An insurance company issues life insurance policies in three separate categories: standard, preferred, and ultra-preferred. Of the company's policyholders, 50% are standard, 40% are preferred, and 10% are ultra-preferred. Each standard policyholder has probability 0.010 of dying in the next year, each preferred policyholder has probability 0.005 of dying in the next year, and each ultra-preferred policyholder has probability 0.001 of dying in the next year.

A policyholder dies in the next year.

What is the probability that the deceased policyholder was ultra-preferred?
solution_steps: Let \(S\), \(R\), and \(U\) denote the standard, preferred, and ultra-preferred categories, respectively. Let \(D\) denote death in the next year.
These categories partition the policyholder population, so \(P(D)=P(S)P(D\mid S)+P(R)P(D\mid R)+P(U)P(D\mid U)\).
The probability of being ultra-preferred and dying is \(P(U\cap D)=0.10(0.001)=0.0001\).
By Bayes' theorem, \(P(U\mid D)=\frac{0.0001}{0.0071}=\frac{1}{71}\approx 0.0141\).
generalization: For mutually exclusive and exhaustive categories \(C_1,\ldots,C_n\), \(P(C_k\mid D)=\frac{P(C_k)P(D\mid C_k)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}P(C_i)P(D\mid C_i)}\), provided \(P(D)>0\). Weight each category's event probability by its population share before normalizing.

title: Exercise 27
statement:
[SOA 18; S03.08] An auto insurance company insures drivers of all ages. An actuary compiled the following statistics on the company's insured drivers:

Age 16–20: probability of accident = 0.06; portion of insured drivers = 0.08.
Age 21–30: probability of accident = 0.03; portion of insured drivers = 0.15.
Age 31–65: probability of accident = 0.02; portion of insured drivers = 0.49.
Age 66–99: probability of accident = 0.04; portion of insured drivers = 0.28.

A randomly selected driver that the company insures has an accident.

Calculate the probability that the driver was 16–20.
solution_steps: Let \(T\) denote a driver aged 16–20 and \(A\) denote an accident. We want \(P(T\mid A)\), whereas the table gives \(P(A\mid T)=0.06\).
The probability that a driver is aged 16–20 and has an accident is \(P(T\cap A)=P(T)P(A\mid T)=0.08(0.06)=0.0048\).
By Bayes' theorem, \(P(T\mid A)=\frac{0.0048}{0.0303}=\frac{16}{101}\approx 0.158416\). Rounded to two decimal places, the answer is \(0.16\).
generalization: When a table gives population shares \(w_i\) and conditional accident probabilities \(a_i\), the overall accident probability is \(\sum_i w_i a_i\). Given an accident, the probability of belonging to group \(k\) is \(\frac{w_k a_k}{\sum_i w_i a_i}\). Do not confuse \(P(A\mid C_k)\) with \(P(C_k\mid A)\).

title: Exercise 28
statement: Each year, there is a 40% probability of no hurricanes hitting Stormy Island. The probability of exactly one hurricane hitting Stormy Island equals the probability of 2 or more hurricanes hitting Stormy Island. What is the mode number of hurricanes that hit Stormy Island in a year?
choices: It cannot be determined from the information given.
solution_steps: Let \(N\) denote the number of hurricanes in a year. We know \(P(N=0)=0.4\) and \(P(N=1)=P(N\geq 2)\).
The events \(N=0\), \(N=1\), and \(N\geq 2\) partition all possible outcomes. Therefore, \(0.4+P(N=1)+P(N\geq 2)=1\).
Since the last two probabilities are equal, \(P(N=1)=P(N\geq 2)=0.3\).
For every integer \(n\geq 2\), \(P(N=n)\leq P(N\geq 2)=0.3\).
Thus \(P(N=0)=0.4\) is strictly larger than the probability of any other individual value. The unique mode is \(0\).
generalization: A mode of a discrete random variable is a value maximizing its probability mass. Even without knowing every individual probability, a mode can be identified if each remaining probability is bounded above by a number smaller than the candidate's probability.

title: Exercise 29
statement: Suppose that \(N\) is a random variable with \(P(N=0)=0.1\), \(P(N=1)=0.3\), \(P(N=2)=0.2\), and \(P(N=3)=0.4\). Find the mode of \(N\).
choices: It cannot be determined from the information given.
solution_steps: The probabilities sum to \(0.1+0.3+0.2+0.4=1\), so these values account for the entire distribution.
A mode is a value of \(N\) with the largest probability.
The largest probability is \(0.4\), which occurs at \(N=3\). Therefore, the mode is \(3\).
generalization: For a discrete probability mass function \(p(n)\), the modes are the values attaining \(\max_n p(n)\). The mode is the value of the random variable, not the probability at that value. Multiple values can tie for the maximum.

title: Exercise 30
statement: Each year, there is a 40% probability of no hurricanes hitting Stormy Island. The probability of exactly one hurricane hitting Stormy Island equals the probability of 2 or more hurricanes hitting Stormy Island. What is the median number of hurricanes that hit Stormy Island in a year?
choices: It cannot be determined from the information given.
solution_steps: Let \(N\) denote the number of hurricanes in a year. We have \(P(N=0)=0.4\) and \(P(N=1)=P(N\geq 2)\).
Since probabilities sum to 1, \(0.4+2P(N=1)=1\). Hence \(P(N=1)=0.3\) and \(P(N\geq 2)=0.3\).
The cumulative probabilities are \(P(N\leq 0)=0.4\) and \(P(N\leq 1)=0.4+0.3=0.7\). The cumulative probability crosses 0.5 at \(1\).
Indeed, \(P(N\leq 1)=0.7\geq 0.5\) and \(P(N\geq 1)=0.6\geq 0.5\), so \(1\) is a median.
Any number below 1 has at most 0.4 probability below or equal to it, and any number above 1 has at most 0.3 probability above or equal to it. Therefore, the unique median is \(1\).
generalization: A median \(m\) satisfies both \(P(X\leq m)\geq 1/2\) and \(P(X\geq m)\geq 1/2\). For a discrete distribution, use cumulative probabilities rather than choosing the most likely value. A median need not be unique.

title: Exercise 31
statement: A toy company sells exactly three distinct types of toys: cars, which cost $5, trains, which cost $10, and spaceships, which cost $25. If the number of cars sold is twice the number of trains sold, but half of the number of spaceships sold, what is the average price per toy?
solution_steps: Let the number of trains sold be \(t\). Then the number of cars sold is \(2t\). Since cars are half as numerous as spaceships, the number of spaceships sold is \(4t\).
The sales ratio for cars, trains, and spaceships is therefore \(2:1:4\), with \(7t\) toys sold in total.
For a randomly selected toy among those sold, the price probabilities are \(P(X=5)=2/7\), \(P(X=10)=1/7\), and \(P(X=25)=4/7\).
The average price is \(E[X]=5\left(\frac{2}{7}\right)+10\left(\frac{1}{7}\right)+25\left(\frac{4}{7}\right)=\frac{120}{7}\approx 17.142857\).
Rounded to one decimal place, the average price per toy is $17.1.
generalization: If values \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\) occur in proportions \(r_1:\cdots:r_k\), their weighted mean is \(\frac{\sum_i r_i x_i}{\sum_i r_i}\). A simple unweighted average is appropriate only when all values have equal weights.

title: Exercise 32
statement: Suppose that each side of a six-sided die is equally likely to come up. If the numbers on the first five sides are 2, 2, 3, 5 and 7, and the expected value of a roll is 4, what is the number on the sixth face?
solution_steps: Let \(x\) denote the number on the sixth face and \(Y\) denote the result of a roll.
Each face has probability \(1/6\), so \(E[Y]=\frac{2+2+3+5+7+x}{6}=\frac{19+x}{6}\).
Using \(E[Y]=4\), we obtain \(19+x=24\).
Therefore, the number on the sixth face is \(x=5\).
generalization: For \(k\) equally likely faces with labels \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\), the expected value is \(\mu=\frac{1}{k}\sum_i x_i\). One missing label is \(x_k=k\mu-\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}x_i\). Repeated labels must be counted once for each face on which they appear.

topic: Discrete Random Variables: Functions and Moments
title: Exercise 33
statement: Suppose that \(P(N=n)\) is proportional to \(n\) for \(n=1,2,3,4\), and is 0 otherwise. Find \(E[(N-2)^2]\).
solution_steps: Write \(P(N=n)=cn\) for \(n=1,2,3,4\). Normalization requires \(c(1+2+3+4)=1\), so \(c=1/10\).
Thus the probabilities for \(N=1,2,3,4\) are \(0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4\), respectively.
Alternative method: expand \((N-2)^2=N^2-4N+4\). By linearity, \(E[(N-2)^2]=E[N^2]-4E[N]+4\).
Substitution gives \(E[(N-2)^2]=10-4(3)+4=2\).
generalization: For a discrete random variable, \(E[g(N)]=\sum_n g(n)P(N=n)\). In particular, \(E[(N-a)^2]=E[N^2]-2aE[N]+a^2=\operatorname{Var}(N)+(E[N]-a)^2\), assuming a finite second moment. In general, \(E[(N-a)^2]\neq(E[N]-a)^2\).

title: Exercise 34
statement:
[SOA 475] Let \(X\) represent the number of defective parts in a shipment of four.

\[P(X\geq x)=\frac{1}{4}\left(1-\frac{x-2}{3}\right)^2,\qquad x=1,2,3,4.\]

Calculate \(E[X]\).
solution_steps: Since \(X\) counts defective parts in a shipment of four, its possible values are \(0,1,2,3,4\).
For a nonnegative integer-valued random variable, the tail-sum formula gives \(E[X]=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}P(X\geq k)\). Here, all terms beyond \(k=4\) are zero.
Evaluate the given probabilities: \(P(X\geq 1)=\frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^2=\frac{4}{9}\), \(P(X\geq 2)=\frac{1}{4}\), \(P(X\geq 3)=\frac{1}{9}\), and \(P(X\geq 4)=\frac{1}{36}\).
Therefore, \(E[X]=\frac{4}{9}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{36}=\frac{16+9+4+1}{36}=\frac{5}{6}\approx 0.833333\). The answer rounded to two decimal places is \(0.83\).
Alternative method: obtain the probability mass function by subtracting consecutive tails, \(P(X=k)=P(X\geq k)-P(X\geq k+1)\). Use \(P(X\geq 0)=1\) and \(P(X\geq 5)=0\).
Then \(E[X]=0\left(\frac{5}{9}\right)+1\left(\frac{7}{36}\right)+2\left(\frac{5}{36}\right)+3\left(\frac{3}{36}\right)+4\left(\frac{1}{36}\right)=\frac{30}{36}=\frac{5}{6}\).
generalization: For a nonnegative integer-valued random variable, \(E[X]=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}P(X\geq k)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}P(X>k)\). The starting index depends on whether the inequality is weak or strict. Recover individual probabilities using \(P(X=k)=P(X\geq k)-P(X\geq k+1)\).

title: Exercise 35
statement:
A customer loyalty program tracks the number of times a customer visits a particular store in a month. Let \(X\) be the number of visits a randomly chosen customer makes in a month. The probabilities that a customer makes more than \(k\) visits are as follows:

\(P(X>0)=0.80\)
\(P(X>1)=0.50\)
\(P(X>2)=0.20\)
\(P(X>3)=0.05\)
\(P(X>4)=0\)

Find the expected number of visits a customer makes in a month.
solution_steps: Since \(X\) is a nonnegative integer-valued random variable, use \(E[X]=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}P(X>k)\).
The given condition \(P(X>4)=0\) implies that all tail probabilities for \(k\geq 4\) are zero.
Therefore, \(E[X]=0.80+0.50+0.20+0.05=1.55\) visits per month.
Alternative check: \(P(X=0)=1-0.80=0.20\). Subtracting consecutive tails gives \(P(X=1)=0.30\), \(P(X=2)=0.30\), \(P(X=3)=0.15\), and \(P(X=4)=0.05\).
generalization: If \(S(k)=P(X>k)\) for a nonnegative integer-valued random variable, then \(E[X]=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}S(k)\). Also, \(P(X=0)=1-S(0)\) and \(P(X=k)=S(k-1)-S(k)\) for \(k\geq 1\). Tail probabilities are cumulative probabilities, so they should not be treated as individual probability masses.

title: Exercise 36
statement:
Suppose that \(X\) can only take on one of the four possible values from the probability distribution given below:

\(P(X=1)=0.2\)
\(P(X=3)=0.3\)
\(P(X=5)=0.4\)
\(P(X=9)=p\)

What is the variance of \(X\)?
solution_steps: The probabilities must sum to 1, so \(p=1-0.2-0.3-0.4=0.1\).
Therefore, \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[X^2]-(E[X])^2=21-4^2=5\).
generalization: For a discrete distribution, first determine any missing probabilities using normalization. Then calculate \(E[X]=\sum_x xp(x)\) and \(E[X^2]=\sum_x x^2p(x)\). The variance is \(E[X^2]-(E[X])^2\), not the second raw moment alone.

title: Exercise 37
statement: Given that \(E[Y]=2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=3\), find \(\operatorname{Var}(3Y+4)\).
solution_steps: For constants \(a\) and \(b\), \(\operatorname{Var}(aY+b)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(Y)\).
Adding 4 does not change the variance, while multiplying by 3 multiplies the variance by \(3^2=9\).
Therefore, \(\operatorname{Var}(3Y+4)=9(3)=27\). The given mean is not needed.
generalization: For a random variable with finite variance, \(\operatorname{Var}(aY+b)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(Y)\) and \(\operatorname{SD}(aY+b)=|a|\operatorname{SD}(Y)\). Translation changes the mean but leaves the variance unchanged.

topic: Discrete Random Variables: Coefficient of Variation
title: Exercise 38
statement: Let \(X\) be a random variable whose distribution is \(P(X=1)=P(X=3)=1/4\) and \(P(X=8)=1/2\). What is the coefficient of variation of \(X\)?
solution_steps: Calculate the mean: \(E[X]=1\left(\frac14\right)+3\left(\frac14\right)+8\left(\frac12\right)=5\).
Calculate the second raw moment: \(E[X^2]=1^2\left(\frac14\right)+3^2\left(\frac14\right)+8^2\left(\frac12\right)=34.5\).
The variance is \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=34.5-5^2=9.5\), so \(\operatorname{SD}(X)=\sqrt{9.5}\).
Since the mean is positive, \(\operatorname{CV}(X)=\frac{\operatorname{SD}(X)}{E[X]}=\frac{\sqrt{9.5}}{5}\approx 0.616441\).
Rounded to two decimal places, the coefficient of variation is \(0.62\).
generalization: For a positive mean, \(\operatorname{CV}(X)=\frac{\sqrt{E[X^2]-(E[X])^2}}{E[X]}\). It measures dispersion relative to the mean and has no units. Use the standard deviation in the numerator, not the variance.

title: Exercise 39
statement: Let \(N\) be a randomly selected three-digit number, with each integer from 100 through 999 equally likely. What is \(E[N]\)?
solution_steps: There are \(999-100+1=900\) three-digit positive integers, each with probability \(1/900\).
Using the arithmetic-series formula, \(\sum_{n=100}^{999}n=\frac{900(100+999)}{2}\).
Equivalently, pairing the smallest and largest values gives \(100+999=101+998=\cdots=1099\). Each pair has average \(1099/2=549.5\).
generalization: If \(N\) is uniform on the consecutive integers \(a,a+1,\ldots,b\), then \(E[N]=(a+b)/2\). This follows directly from the sum of an arithmetic series and requires equal probabilities.

title: Exercise 40
statement: Let \(Y\) be the outcome of the roll of a fair four-sided die numbered 1 through 4. What is the coefficient of variation of \(25+100Y\)?
solution_steps: Its variance is \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=100^2\operatorname{Var}(Y)=10000(1.25)=12500\).
Therefore, \(\operatorname{CV}(Z)=\frac{\sqrt{12500}}{275}\approx 0.406558\), which rounds to \(0.41\).
generalization: For \(Z=aX+b\) with positive mean, \(\operatorname{CV}(Z)=\frac{|a|\operatorname{SD}(X)}{aE[X]+b}\). Positive scaling alone preserves the coefficient of variation, but adding a constant generally changes it.

title: Exercise 41
statement: An old computer network had 5-character user names. Each of the first 2 characters could be any one of the 26 letters of the alphabet, the 3rd and 4th characters could be any one of the 10 digits, and the 5th character could be any letter or digit. How many possible user names were there?
solution_steps: Each of the first two positions has 26 possible letters. No restriction prohibits repetition.
Each of the third and fourth positions has 10 possible digits.
The fifth position has \(26+10=36\) possibilities because letters and digits are disjoint categories.
By the multiplication principle, the total number of user names is \(26\times26\times10\times10\times36=2{,}433{,}600\).
generalization: If each valid partial sequence has \(n_i\) choices for position \(i\), the total number of complete sequences is \(\prod_i n_i\). Add counts for disjoint alternatives within a position, and multiply counts across successive positions.

title: Exercise 42
statement:
Find the number of 4-digit passcodes that satisfy both of the following conditions:

The first and second digits must each be one of 3 through 9.

The third and fourth digits can be any of 0 through 9, but must be different from each other.
solution_steps: The digits from 3 through 9 give \(9-3+1=7\) choices for the first position.
The second position also has 7 choices. The first two digits are allowed to match.
The third position has 10 choices, from 0 through 9.
For each choice of the third digit, the fourth position has 9 choices because it must exclude that digit.
Therefore, the number of valid passcodes is \(7\times7\times10\times9=4{,}410\).
generalization: Apply distinctness restrictions only where stated. Two ordered positions chosen from \(m\) symbols have \(m^2\) possibilities when repetition is allowed and \(m(m-1)\) when their symbols must differ.

topic: Conditional Probability and Sampling Without Replacement
title: Exercise 43
statement: Urn I contains seven red and three black balls, and urn II contains four red and five black balls. After a randomly selected ball is transferred from urn I to urn II, two balls are randomly drawn from urn II without replacement. What is the probability that both balls drawn from urn II are red?
solution_steps: Condition on the color of the transferred ball. A red ball is transferred with probability \(7/10\), and a black ball with probability \(3/10\).
If a red ball is transferred, urn II contains 5 red and 5 black balls. The conditional probability of drawing two red balls is \(\frac{5}{10}\frac{4}{9}=\frac{2}{9}\).
If a black ball is transferred, urn II contains 4 red and 6 black balls. The conditional probability of drawing two red balls is \(\frac{4}{10}\frac{3}{9}=\frac{2}{15}\).
By the law of total probability, the desired probability is \(\frac{7}{10}\frac{2}{9}+\frac{3}{10}\frac{2}{15}=\frac{7}{45}+\frac{1}{25}=\frac{44}{225}\).
generalization: When a transfer changes an urn's composition, condition on what was transferred before calculating the sampling probability. For an urn containing \(r\) red balls among \(n\) balls, the probability of two red draws without replacement is \(\binom{r}{2}/\binom{n}{2}=r(r-1)/(n(n-1))\).

title: Exercise 44
statement: If thirteen cards are randomly chosen without replacement from an ordinary 52-card deck, what is the probability of obtaining exactly three aces?
solution_steps: There are \(\binom{52}{13}\) equally likely unordered hands of 13 cards.
Choose exactly 3 of the deck's 4 aces in \(\binom{4}{3}\) ways.
The remaining 10 cards must all be non-aces. There are 48 non-aces, giving \(\binom{48}{10}\) choices.
Therefore, the probability is \(\frac{\binom{4}{3}\binom{48}{10}}{\binom{52}{13}}\).
Do not select the remaining cards from all 49 cards left after choosing three aces: that would allow the fourth ace and violate the requirement of exactly three aces.
generalization: For a sample of size \(n\) drawn uniformly without replacement from \(N\) objects containing \(K\) successes, the probability of exactly \(k\) successes is \(\frac{\binom{K}{k}\binom{N-K}{n-k}}{\binom{N}{n}}\), for feasible values of \(k\).

title: Exercise 45
statement: [110.S88.16] What is the probability that a hand of five cards chosen randomly and without replacement from a standard deck of 52 cards contains the king of spades, exactly one other king, and exactly two queens?
solution_steps: There are \(\binom{52}{5}\) equally likely five-card hands.
The king of spades is required, so there is exactly one way to include that card.
Choose the other king from the remaining three kings in \(\binom{3}{1}\) ways.
Choose exactly two of the four queens in \(\binom{4}{2}\) ways.
The fifth card must be neither a king nor a queen. There are \(52-4-4=44\) such cards.
The number of favorable hands is \(\binom{3}{1}\binom{4}{2}\binom{44}{1}=3\cdot6\cdot44=792\). Therefore, the probability is \(\frac{792}{\binom{52}{5}}\).
generalization: When a particular card is required, fix that card first and count the remaining choices. For exact rank counts, all leftover cards must come from outside the constrained ranks. Use unordered combinations consistently in both numerator and denominator.

title: Exercise 46
statement: In a game, a player flips 2 fair coins and loses if both are heads. Assume all coin flips are independent. What is the probability that a player loses exactly 3 times in 5 plays of the game?
solution_steps: In one play, the player loses only on two heads, so \(p=P(\text{loss})=\frac12\frac12=\frac14\).
The probability of not losing a play is \(1-p=3/4\).
Let \(L\) be the number of losses in five independent plays. Then \(L\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(5,1/4)\).
There are \(\binom{5}{3}=10\) ways to choose which three plays are losses.
Thus \(P(L=3)=\binom{5}{3}\left(\frac14\right)^3\left(\frac34\right)^2=10\cdot\frac{3^2}{4^5}=\frac{45}{512}\).
The probability of losing a play is \(1/4\), not \(1/2\): a play consists of two coin flips.
generalization: For \(n\) independent trials with a constant event probability \(p\), the number of occurrences is binomial: \(P(X=k)=\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}\). First identify what constitutes one trial and calculate its event probability.

title: Exercise 47
statement: [110.S90.28] I have two unfair coins: a gold coin that comes up heads with probability 0.3, and a silver coin that comes up heads with probability 0.1. If I flip the gold coin 5 times and the silver coin 10 times, what is the probability that the gold coin comes up heads exactly 3 times and the silver coin comes up heads exactly 6 times? Assume all flips are independent.
solution_steps: Let \(G\) and \(S\) count heads from the gold and silver coins. Then \(G\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(5,0.3)\) and \(S\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(10,0.1)\).
The gold-coin probability is \(P(G=3)=\binom{5}{3}(0.3)^3(0.7)^2\).
The silver-coin probability is \(P(S=6)=\binom{10}{6}(0.1)^6(0.9)^4\).
Because the two collections of flips are independent, \(P(G=3,S=6)=P(G=3)P(S=6)\).
generalization: For independent binomial counts, multiply the individual probabilities to obtain a joint probability. Do not combine trials with different success probabilities into a single ordinary binomial model.

title: Exercise 48
statement:
[SOA 37; S00.40] A company prices its hurricane insurance using the following assumptions:

1. In any calendar year, there can be at most one hurricane.
2. In any calendar year, the probability of a hurricane is 0.05.
3. The number of hurricanes in any calendar year is independent of the number of hurricanes in any other calendar year.

Using the company's assumptions, calculate the probability that there are fewer than 3 hurricanes in a 20-year period.
solution_steps: Each year is an independent Bernoulli trial with hurricane probability \(0.05\). Thus the total number of hurricanes satisfies \(X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(20,0.05)\).
Fewer than 3 hurricanes means \(X=0,1,2\), so \(P(X<3)=P(X=0)+P(X=1)+P(X=2)\).
The zero-hurricane probability is \(P(X=0)=(0.95)^{20}\approx 0.358486\).
The one-hurricane probability is \(P(X=1)=\binom{20}{1}(0.05)(0.95)^{19}\approx 0.377354\).
The two-hurricane probability is \(P(X=2)=\binom{20}{2}(0.05)^2(0.95)^{18}\approx 0.188677\).
Adding gives \(P(X<3)\approx 0.924516\), which rounds to \(0.92\).
generalization: For \(X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)\) and an integer threshold \(r\), \(P(X<r)=\sum_{k=0}^{r-1}\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}\). Distinguish fewer than \(r\) from at most \(r\), which includes the term \(X=r\).

title: Exercise 49
statement: A drawer contains four white socks, six red socks, and two black socks. Two socks are taken at random from the drawer without replacement. What is the probability that both socks will be the same color?
solution_steps: There are \(4+6+2=12\) socks, giving \(\binom{12}{2}=66\) equally likely unordered pairs.
The favorable cases are mutually exclusive: two white socks, two red socks, or two black socks.
Their counts are \(\binom{4}{2}=6\), \(\binom{6}{2}=15\), and \(\binom{2}{2}=1\), respectively.
Therefore, \(P(\text{same color})=\frac{6+15+1}{66}=\frac{22}{66}=\frac13\).
Equivalently, using sequential draws gives \(\frac4{12}\frac3{11}+\frac6{12}\frac5{11}+\frac2{12}\frac1{11}=\frac13\).
generalization: If a population contains \(n_i\) objects of category \(i\), with total \(N=\sum_i n_i\geq2\), two uniform draws without replacement have the same category with probability \(\frac{\sum_i\binom{n_i}{2}}{\binom{N}{2}}=\sum_i\frac{n_i(n_i-1)}{N(N-1)}\).

title: Exercise 50
statement: A drawer contains four white socks, six red socks, and two black socks. Two socks are taken at random from the drawer with replacement. What is the probability that both socks will be the same color?
solution_steps: With replacement and independent random draws, the color probabilities remain \(P(W)=4/12\), \(P(R)=6/12\), and \(P(B)=2/12\).
The probability of two white socks is \((4/12)^2=1/9\).
The probability of two red socks is \((6/12)^2=1/4\), and the probability of two black socks is \((2/12)^2=1/36\).
These cases are mutually exclusive, so \(P(\text{same color})=\frac19+\frac14+\frac1{36}=\frac{14}{36}=\frac7{18}\).
Unlike sampling without replacement, the second draw still has 12 available socks and the original color counts.
generalization: For two independent draws with category probabilities \(p_1,\ldots,p_m\), the probability of matching categories is \(\sum_{i=1}^{m}p_i^2\). Multiply probabilities within each matching case, then add over the mutually exclusive categories.

title: Exercise 51
statement: [110.S88.35] A box contains 35 gems, of which ten are real diamonds and 25 are fake diamonds. Gems are randomly taken out of the box, one at a time without replacement. What is the probability that exactly two fakes are selected before the second real diamond is selected?
solution_steps: Exactly two fakes before the second real diamond means that the fourth draw is real, while the first three draws contain exactly one real diamond and two fakes.
Writing \(R\) for real and \(F\) for fake, the possible sequences are \(RFFR\), \(FRFR\), and \(FFRR\).
Each sequence has probability \(\frac{10\cdot9\cdot25\cdot24}{35\cdot34\cdot33\cdot32}\). The order of the numerator factors changes, but their product is the same.
Adding the three mutually exclusive sequences gives \(3\frac{10\cdot9\cdot25\cdot24}{35\cdot34\cdot33\cdot32}=\frac{675}{5236}\).
Alternatively, the probability of one real and two fakes in the first three draws is \(\frac{\binom{10}{1}\binom{25}{2}}{\binom{35}{3}}\). Given that event, 9 of the remaining 32 gems are real.

Thus the answer is also \(\frac{\binom{10}{1}\binom{25}{2}}{\binom{35}{3}}\frac9{32}\). Merely requiring two real diamonds among the first four draws does not enforce that the fourth draw is the second real diamond.
generalization: In uniform sampling without replacement from \(N\) objects containing \(K\) successes, the probability of exactly \(f\) failures before the \(r\)th success is \(\frac{\binom{K}{r-1}\binom{N-K}{f}}{\binom{N}{r+f-1}}\frac{K-r+1}{N-r-f+1}\), for \(1\leq r\leq K\) and \(0\leq f\leq N-K\). This is a negative hypergeometric stopping problem: the last draw must be a success.

title: Exercise 52
statement: [110.S88.07] A bag contains 10 balls, 5 of which are white, 3 are red, and two are black. If three balls are drawn with replacement from the bag, what is the probability that one ball of each color is drawn?
solution_steps: The independent draws have constant color probabilities \(p_W=5/10\), \(p_R=3/10\), and \(p_B=2/10\).
We need category counts \((1,1,1)\) in three draws, so use the multinomial formula.
There are \(\frac{3!}{1!1!1!}=6\) possible orders of the three colors.
Each order has probability \(\frac5{10}\frac3{10}\frac2{10}=0.03\).
Therefore, the desired probability is \(6(0.03)=0.18\).
generalization: For \(n\) independent trials with constant category probabilities \(p_i\), the probability of counts \(k_i\) summing to \(n\) is \(\frac{n!}{\prod_i k_i!}\prod_i p_i^{k_i}\). The factorial coefficient accounts for all orders producing those counts.

title: Exercise 53
statement: [110.F86.16] A random sample of size 6 is selected with replacement from an urn that contains 10 red, 5 white, and 5 blue balls. What is the probability that the sample contains 2 balls of each color?
solution_steps: There are 20 balls. On each independent draw, the color probabilities are \(p_R=10/20=1/2\), \(p_W=5/20=1/4\), and \(p_B=5/20=1/4\).
We need exactly two occurrences of each color in six draws.
The number of color sequences with these counts is \(\frac{6!}{2!2!2!}=90\).
Each such sequence has probability \(\left(\frac12\right)^2\left(\frac14\right)^2\left(\frac14\right)^2=\frac1{1024}\).
Therefore, the probability is \(90\cdot\frac1{1024}=\frac{45}{512}\).
generalization: When repeated independent draws must produce specified counts in several categories, use one multinomial coefficient to count the possible orders. Multiplying separate binomial probabilities for the category counts is incorrect because those counts are dependent and must sum to the fixed sample size.
